claims.statement: The difference in variances between two trial arms can be estimated from summary data alone (sample sizes and SDs) with a standard error, and meta-analysed with standard inverse-variance methods; this is proposed here alongside the ratio of variances, the log ratio of SDs and the log ratio of coefficients of variation.
claims.scope: Continuous outcomes, two-arm parallel trials, summary data. Demonstrated on 19 RCTs of computer-based psychological treatment for depression and 22 statin trials from a Cochrane review.

our_assessment.why: Correct and, importantly for this corpus, PRIOR. Two of my records asserted that the psychiatric literature does not report D and read as though the method were unavailable. The first half is true of the applications; the second is false -- this is a 2021 paper in a general epidemiology journal with deposited R code. Corrected in place in ploderl2019 and winkelbeiner2019 and in the area file. The lesson recorded with it: I checked prior art for the claim I was least sure of (the floor mechanism, where I found Hope et al. 2019) and skipped it for the claim the whole argument rested on. Centrality, not confidence, should trigger the search.

claims.statement: The coefficient of variation should be compared between arms only when the outcome is on a ratio scale with a meaningful zero; the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and the Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale are interval scales and do not qualify.
claims.scope: Stated in Table 1 as a requirement of both CoV methods and argued in the Methods; the two named violations are citations to the psychiatric variability meta-analyses.

our_assessment.why: Correct, and it is the substance of what I recorded as a new finding on ploderl2019#c2 five years later. What remains mine is the exact form: lnCVR minus lnVR equals the log ratio of arm means EXACTLY (Nakagawa's small-sample corrections are identical in both and cancel), measured to 2.8e-16 over 169 trials -- so lnCVR carries no information beyond lnVR and the treatment effect, which is stronger than 'the scale does not support it'. And the consequence they do not draw: the SIGN of a CVR result is set by the reporting convention, 0.82 on change scores and 1.15 on endpoint scores in the same paper on the same drugs.

claims.statement: A correlation between the mean and the SD across trials does not indicate that the coefficient of variation differs between arms; the CoV should be used only when the scale qualifies, irrespective of the observed correlation.
claims.scope: Simulation in eAppendix 3, two conditions (same CoV in both arms, different CoV in both arms). The conclusion is stated in the body; the parameters are in the gated appendix.

our_assessment.why: Accepted on the authors' report; the simulation itself is gated (a4) and has not been reproduced here. It is the substance of what I recorded as ploderl2019#c3. What remains mine on that corpus is quantitative and specific: of the r(M,SD) = 0.55 that Ploderl & Hengartner cite as their justification, 75% is between-SCALE mixing (within-scale pooled r = 0.135 across HAMD17/21/24 and MADRS), and the within-trial between-arm correlation that would actually license the division is +0.110 with p = 0.154.

claims.statement: MARIA 2026: their difference-in-variances estimator is biased when the arms differ in size, and the bias has the same sign as the finding they report.
claims.scope: MetaAnalysis.R lines 129-144 compute est_diff_SE as 2 s1^4/(n1-1) + 2 s2^4/(n2-1) and pass it to metagen for inverse-variance pooling. Calibrated on a real 169-trial corpus with D = 0 by construction, 500 simulated corpora per cell.

our_assessment.why: Accepted as a property of the estimator, demonstrated with three falsifiable predictions of its mechanism that all held (equal arms shrink the bias to +0.064; swapping the arms reverses it to -0.567; a weight built from the across-arm pooled variance removes it, -0.003 with 96.6% coverage). NARROWER because I have NOT recomputed their two applied examples -- their deposit carries the code and not the trial-level data. Their headline observation is that variance was smaller in the intervention arm in both meta-analyses, which is the direction this bias moves when the intervention arm is the larger one, but pointing at a direction is not showing an effect. Nothing here says their applied results are wrong; it says their estimator has an untested bias whose sign coincides with their finding, and that recomputing is a day's work with published data.

claims.statement: Lower variance in the intervention arm may be partly because the outcome scale is bounded at zero and floor or ceiling effects reduce variance.
claims.scope: One sentence in the Discussion, about the BDI (range 0-63) in their single trial and their first meta-analysis. Unquantified.

our_assessment.why: Correct and prior to my 'fifth axis of non-identification'. They name the mechanism; they do not quantify it, and my work adds three things that are not here: the governing dimensionless parameter z = (mean headroom - mean improvement)/SD(improvement); the shrinkage curve statlib.floor_shrinkage(z, headroom_dispersion); and the finding that the DIRECTION REVERSES above about 1.5 improvement-SDs of headroom dispersion, so 'a bound reduces variance' is a statement about a regime rather than a law. Also the size on real corpora: 1-3%, which is the magnitude of every effect the psychiatric literature has reported.

claims.statement: Difference in variances should be meta-analysed only when all trials use the same outcome scale; where scales differ, the ratio of variances is the appropriate summary.

our_assessment.why: Correct and prior. I violated it and then caught it independently: a pooled D of -0.384 in mccutcheon2022#c6 mixed squared HAMD17, HAMD21, HAMD24 and MADRS points, and its own unit string read 'squared HAMD/MADRS points'. Marked superseded 2026-09-06 with per-scale values. Their sentence would have prevented it.

relations.why: Not a citation either author made. Mills et al. state in 2021 that the coefficient of variation requires a ratio scale and that HAMD/MADRS do not qualify, citing the psychiatric variability meta-analyses directly; Ploderl & Hengartner compute and interpret a CVR on exactly those scales in 2019 and their supplement repeats it on endpoint scores.
relations.asymmetric_note: Chronology runs the wrong way for a citation -- Mills is later -- so this edge means 'the later paper settles the earlier one's method', not 'the earlier paper ignored it'.

relations.why: Their one-sentence note that a bounded scale reduces variance in the arm that improves more is the mechanism I derived and quantified there. The quantification stands; the priority does not.

Both hold that a difference in variance between arms is evidence of effect modification only after other explanations -- noncompliance, differential engagement, model misspecification, within-person variability -- are excluded, and both say the exclusion needs individual data.
The corrected weight verified in this corpus (statlib.var_diff weight='pooled') was developed against the estimator their code implements, and was applied there to supersede a unit-mixed pooled D.

My record there presented the bounded-scale mechanism as a fifth axis of non-identification that this literature had not named. Mills et al. name it in 2021. The quantification in that record stands; the priority claim is corrected in place there.
relations.asymmetric_note: This edge corrects MY record, not the Winkelbeiner paper, which does not discuss the bounded scale at all.

open_questions: Recompute their two applied meta-analyses -- 19 computer-based therapy RCTs and 22 statin trials from a Cochrane review -- with the corrected weight. Their deposit has the code and not the trial-level data; both source reviews are published and carry mean, SD and n per arm, which is all that is needed.
eAppendix 3, the simulation severing the mean-SD correlation from the CoV question, is gated. It is cheap to reproduce from the description in the body and is the evidence for c3.

AnalyseIndividualTrials.R implements Glejser, Levene and the nonconstant-variance linear model -- the individual-data half of this method, absent from this corpus entirely because every psychiatric application works from summary data.

The repository carries NO LICENCE, which formally reserves all rights. Reading it is fine; anything derived from it would need permission. Worth noting because a deposit without a licence is a common and rarely-flagged form of incomplete openness -- and it passes every artifact-badging scheme.
